subject: gravity-explainer

responses: Gravity is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It attracts objects with mass toward each other.
Gravity follows an inverse-square law: the force decreases with the square of the distance between objects.
Einstein described gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy.
Objects stay in orbit because their forward velocity balances gravitational pull, creating a continuous free-fall path.
Orbits are elliptical. The orbiting body moves fastest at its closest point (periapsis) and slowest at its farthest (apoapsis).
The Moon orbits Earth because its sideways velocity of about 1 km/s perfectly balances Earth's gravitational acceleration.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object — it doesn't change. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass — it varies by location.
On the Moon, your mass is the same but you weigh about 1/6th as much because lunar gravity is weaker.
Mass is measured in kilograms. Weight is measured in newtons. A 70 kg person weighs about 686 N on Earth but only 114 N on the Moon.
A gravity well is the gravitational potential field around a massive object. The deeper the well, the more energy needed to escape it.
Think of gravity wells as funnels in spacetime. Planets and moons sit in the Sun's well. Spacecraft must climb out of Earth's well to travel elsewhere.
Escape velocity is the speed needed to climb out of a gravity well completely: 11.2 km/s for Earth, 2.4 km/s for the Moon.

memories: Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces but dominates at large scales because it has infinite range and is always attractive.
Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation: F = G(m1)(m2)/r^2 where G is the gravitational constant.
Einstein's general relativity (1915) redefined gravity: mass-energy tells spacetime how to curve, curved spacetime tells matter how to move.
The Moon's orbit is a perfect real-world demonstration: its 1.022 km/s orbital velocity exactly balances Earth's gravitational acceleration at that distance (384,400 km).
Gravitational waves were first directly detected in 2015 by LIGO, confirming a prediction Einstein made 100 years earlier.
Microgravity on the ISS is not zero-gravity — astronauts experience about 90% of Earth's surface gravity but are in continuous free-fall, creating the sensation of weightlessness.
response: Gravity is a fundamental force attracting objects with mass. Newton described it mathematically as F=G(m1)(m2)/r^2. Einstein redefined it as spacetime curvature. It governs orbits, determines weight, and creates gravity wells. The Moon's orbit demonstrates the perfect balance between velocity and gravitational acceleration.
